subject: Re: Connectivity design options for QuantaRetail private deployment
messages:
From: Oliver Grant <oliver.grant@quantaretail.com>
To: Mina Haddad <mina_haddad@redwood.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>, Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-09-19T13:12:00-04:00
Subject: Connectivity options - quick context and ask

Thanks Mina — quick context from our side and a few asks. We’re finalizing the architecture for QuantaRetail’s private deployment of Redwood inference. High level constraints:
- PCI scope for payment tokenization (we need traffic to stay off public internet whenever possible)
- Multi-region (primary us-east-1, secondary eu-west-1) with active inference in us-east and warm standby in eu-west
- SLO: 99.95% availability, tail latency < 200ms for inference requests from our web apps in us-east
- Ops: we’d prefer a solution that minimizes day-to-day configuration and routing complexity (we don’t want to manage lots of peering links)

We’re evaluating three ingress patterns: VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and site-to-site VPN (IPsec with BGP). Can you provide a recommendation for production (security, reliability, latency and operational overhead) and a short plan for a pilot? I attached our rough network diagram.

Attachments: quantaretail-network-plan.png

Thanks,
Oliver
Head of Platform, QuantaRetail
From: Mina Haddad <mina_haddad@redwood.com>
To: Oliver Grant <oliver.grant@quantaretail.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>, Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-09-19T16:05:00-04:00
Subject: Re: Connectivity options - quick context and ask

Hi Oliver — thanks for the clear constraints and the diagram. High-level recommendation up front: a hybrid approach that uses regional PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for inference/control-plane traffic, an AWS Transit Gateway (or equivalent interconnect) for cross-VPC routing inside the customer account, and a single S2S VPN as a resilient fallback.

Why this mix (short):
- Security: PrivateLink keeps traffic to the Redwood service inside the AWS network fabric (no public internet hop) and is easiest to scope into PCI-sensitive flows that require private endpoints.
- Reliability: PrivateLink endpoints are regional; for multi-region failover you run endpoints per region and rely on application-level failover + a Transit Gateway for internal routing. Transit Gateway reduces the operational burden vs N^2 VPC peering links when you have multiple VPCs or AWS accounts.
- Latency: PrivateLink typically adds a small fixed hop (~1-5ms) versus peering but avoids edge NAT/egress variability. For tight tail-latency requirements we’ve seen PrivateLink + placement of Redwood ingress nodes in the same AZs yield predictable sub-200ms performance for web-origin traffic.
- Ops: VPC peering is simple for single-VPC, single-account setups, but it doesn’t scale well operationally. Managing many peering connections or frequent route table churn is where customers hit the most friction.

Tradeoffs table (high-level):
- VPC peering: Low latency, simple for 1:1 VPCs, but scales poorly (N^2), no central firewalling, route table management overhead.
- PrivateLink: Best for private, whitelisted access; regional endpoints per region, predictable security posture, slightly higher per-GB cost and per-endpoint management.
- S2S VPN: Good as a fallback or for on-prem to cloud; simple to get started but public internet dependent (unless using Direct Connect + VPN), less predictable latency.

Pilot plan (2–3 week):
1) Stand up a per-region PrivateLink connection (us-east-1) from QuantaRetail account to Redwood dedicated ingress. Test auth, certificate pinning, and PCI tokenization flows.
2) Add an S2S VPN (IPsec w/ BGP) as failover. Run 72-hour soak with synthetic traffic + production mirroring to observe failover path latency and observe behavior under load.
3) If you have multiple VPCs/accounts, recommend adding a Transit Gateway and attach VPCs; validate routing and NACL/SG mappings.

I attached a short connectivity matrix that maps requirements to options. Next step — can we schedule a 30 min runbook + security review with your infra/security folks? I’ll loop in Kimberly for onboarding details and Connor for routing/BGP specifics.

Attachments: proposed_connectivity_matrix.csv

Thanks,
Mina Haddad
Sr. Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Thanks Mina — this is helpful. Two clarifying questions from our infra/security teams:
1) Does PrivateLink support cross-region failover natively, or would we need separate endpoints per region + DNS/route-based failover?
2) For our PCI provider we need a stable set of egress IPs for allowlisting. Can Redwood provide static/pinned egress IPs for traffic coming from the inference cluster? If not, what are recommended approaches (NAT gateway in customer account vs Redwood-managed egress)?

Also, curious on cost impact — PrivateLink endpoints per region + Transit Gateway attachment sounds like it could add up. Any ballpark monthly estimates (order of magnitude) for 1M inference requests per month at modest token sizes?

If it helps we can share a small set of traffic profiles — I can loop Aisha from infra.

Oliver
From: Mina Haddad <mina_haddad@redwood.com>
To: Oliver Grant <oliver.grant@quantaretail.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>, Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-09-21T10:37:00-04:00
Subject: Re: Connectivity options - quick context and ask

Oliver — quick answers inline and a short ops note.

> 1) Does PrivateLink support cross-region failover natively?
PrivateLink endpoints are regional. For cross-region failover you need separate endpoints per region and an application-side failover (DNS weighted records or health-aware routing). If you want active-active routing across regions there are two patterns we recommend:
- Per-region PrivateLink endpoints with a client-side failover mechanism (DNS + health checks) — simpler to operate.
- Active-active with cross-region replication and fronting through a multi-region front door (e.g., Route 53 latency/geo routing) combined with Transit Gateway attachments — more complex but provides lower RPO.

> 2) Stable egress IPs for allowlisting?
We don’t expose a large set of stable, customer-dedicated public egress IPs from the hosted plane by default. Options:
- Customer-managed NAT/egress: Host NAT gateways in your VPC and route outbound traffic through them. This gives you stable IPs under your control for PCI allowlisting. Recommended if you need strict allowlisting.
- Dedicated egress appliance: For Dedicated customers we can coordinate a small set of pinned egress IPs and document them in the onboarding packet (this typically requires commitment to a Dedicated or Private deployment model).

Cost/ops notes (ballpark):
- PrivateLink: per-endpoint hour + per-GB data processing. For a single region at moderate volume (1M requests/month, small payloads) customers see low-single-digit kUSD/month for interface endpoints in addition to data processing.
- Transit Gateway: attachment + data processing charges; useful when you have >3 VPCs or multi-account routing to avoid N^2 peering.
- VPN: low hourly cost but variable performance; cheap to pilot.

Recommended immediate next steps:
1) Share a small traffic profile (Aisha can send).
2) We’ll produce a short cost estimate matrix for the three patterns (PrivateLink-first, Peering-first, VPN-fallback).
3) Schedule the 30-min runbook with Kimberly and Connor — I’ve included a short checklist PDF for PrivateLink setup.

I’m happy to join the security review call and walk through PCI scoping implications for tokenization flows.

Best,
Mina
